title: Influence of a low-carbohydrate diet on clinical symptoms, immune homeostasis and sensory function in patients with fibromyalgia syndrome
summary:
Fibromyalgia syndrome (FMS) is a chronic pain disorder that predominantly affects women. FMS is characterized by pain in multiple parts of the body and various accompanying symptoms. The pathophysiology of FMS is not yet fully understood. Thus, treatment options are limited.
In addition to a general pain sensitization and a loss of function of small, peripheral nerve fibers, recent research suggests that a dysregulation in the immune system contributes to the development and maintenance of FMS. Various studies published in high ranked journals showed that such dysregulation in the immune system, specifically a low-grade chronic inflammation, is promoted by a diet high in carbohydrates. Furthermore, there is growing evidence that a low-carbohydrate diet (ketogenic diet) counters this dysregulation of the immune system. Ketone bodies, which are formed as an alternative energy source during carbohydrate restriction, have anti-inflammatory effects. They reduce the low-grade inflammation and improve immune function. Therefore, a ketogenic diet could represent a new therapeutic approach in the treatment of FMS, an area which has been investigated scarcely.
Thus, the aim of this randomized controlled trial is to investigate whether a three-week ketogenic diet in addition to routine care improves FMS symptoms more than routine care alone. Furthermore, it is investigated whether a ketogenic diet improves immune balance as well as immune function and normalizes perception of mechanical and thermal stimuli.
Women 18 years or above who suffer from FMS are randomly assigned to one of two groups. Patients in the intervention group undergo a ketogenic diet under medical supervision for three weeks in addition to routine care. Patients in the control group receive routine care only. Self-tests (point-of-care testing) are used to monitor the production of ketone bodies at regular intervals. Data collection is performed at three time points: before (baseline), directly after and three months after the three-week intervention phase. Patient questionnaires are used to assess symptom severity, health-related quality of life and psychological complaints (depression, anxiety, stress). The body mass index is calculated from body weight and height and the percentage of fat, water, muscle and bone in the body is determined. Additionally, the perception ability and pain sensitivity towards mechanical as well as thermal stimuli are assessed, and blood samples are analyzed for determinants of immune function. 
The primary study endpoint is the group differences in symptom severity directly after the three-week intervention period taking into account potential group differences at baseline.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
• Medically confirmed diagnosis of fibromyalgia syndrome (FMS) according to the criteria of the American college of Rheumatology (ACR)
• Written informed consent
Exclusion criteria:
• current other out- or inpatient treatment for FMS 
• planned other out- or inpatient treatment for FMS during the study period
• Pregnancy or breastfeeding
• Current haemoglobin level < 9 g/dl
• Current use of glucocorticoids
• Last intake of glucocorticoids ≤ 7 days ago
• Use of antidepressants, opioids, anticonvulsants and/or cannabinoids
• Nutritional therapy intervention within the last month
• Rheumatoid or malignant disease
• Severe disease of the internal organs or cardiovascular system
• Severe mental illness
• Current severe or moderate depression (DASS depression score > 13 or clinical diagnosis)
• Acute illness
• Neuropathy or polyneuropathy of other origin
• Untreated thyroid disease
• Serious metabolic disorder (e.g. diabetes mellitus HbA1 C > 48 mmol/mol Hb)
• Autoimmune diseases
• Nickel and/or copper allergy
• Personal relationship to the investigators (family members, relatives)
